problem: LLM-based navigation systems serialize spatial representations (topological graphs, semantic maps) into text, but the linguistic format and choice of contextual cues are treated as neutral engineering decisions, with no controlled analysis of how they shape LLM planning.
motivation: Transformer reasoning depends on how evidence is organized in the token sequence, and cues differ in how well they suit sequential processing (topology vs coordinates). Under-understood biases can systematically derail navigation planners, so controlled, information-equivalent analysis is needed to guide representation design.
key_idea: A dual-interventional framework (representation intervention over format and compression, plus context intervention over cue combination and semantic conflict) under strict information equivalence characterizes LLMs' linguistic inductive bias for navigation planning.
insight: Topology is a robust shield: topology-dominant prompts beat geometry-dominant ones by S_dom of 0.22-0.32 at every model scale. Format is a double-edged sword: hierarchical helps models ≤4B on simple scenes but reverses into overhead at G3-G5, and larger models prefer flat text; clustered is always worst; compression below 50% collapses accuracy in complex scenes. Semantic ambiguity is an Achilles' heel: duplicate labels cut accuracy despite a perfect topology (SAHI ≈0.24 for 4B-32B models).
method: Representation intervention (R1): the same spatial facts are rendered in Flat prose, Hierarchical nested, or Clustered functional-group formats, with strict information equivalence.
Compression intervention (R2): information retention of 100/50/25% per format on Set-B scenes with complexity gradients G1-G5 (6-14 rooms, 4-12 objects, history length 2-11).
Cue combination (C1): Topology-Dominant (explicit graph) vs Geometry-Dominant (coordinates only), scored by the Dominance Score S_dom = Acc_topo - Acc_geom.

Conflict probing (C2): duplicate semantic labels (e.g. two nodes both called 'Bedroom') are injected into a topologically perfect graph with unique IDs, scored by the Semantic Achilles' Heel Index SAHI = (Acc_shield - Acc_conflict)/Acc_shield.
Tasks and scenes: 5 tasks (ObjectLocation, GeometryYN, TopologyYN, ReachYN, PathGen) on 3 synthetic scene sets (A, B, C, 10 scenes each).
Models: Qwen3 0.6B-32B, Llama-3.2 1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B, ChatGPT-5.2 and Gemini-2.5 at temperature 0; 57,500 queries in total.

setting.backbone: Qwen3 (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 14B, 32B), Llama-3.2 (1B, 3B), Llama-3.1-8B, ChatGPT-5.2, Gemini-2.5 (all frozen, prompting only)
setting.model_size: 0.6B to 32B open models plus closed frontier APIs
setting.observation: text-serialized spatial descriptions (topology, geometry, semantics, history) of synthetic scenes
setting.action_space: text answers (Yes/No, object location, generated path over nodes); no low-level actions
setting.simulator: custom synthetic text scene sets (no simulator)
setting.privileged: ground-truth structured scene descriptions (topology, geometry, semantics, history) given as text

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark numbers. Results are reported only in figures (accuracy per tier) plus a few summary values in the text (S_dom 0.22-0.32, SAHI ~0.24, ΔAcc_Avg >0.21).
results: Across five spatial tasks and all model scales, topology-dominant prompts consistently beat geometry-dominant ones (S_dom 0.22-0.32). Hierarchical beats flat only for small models on simple scenes, while clustered is always worst. Duplicate semantic labels hurt most for 4B-32B models (SAHI ≈0.24, ΔAcc >0.21). No comparison to prior systems, as this is an analysis paper.
limitations: Only controlled synthetic text scenes; no real benchmarks with perceptual noise or incomplete annotations
Results are averaged over models and scenes and shown in figures, with no per-model numbers or significance tests; mechanistic attention explanations are asserted, not measured
Only one conflict type (duplicate semantic labels) and small scene sets (10 scenes each)
